6.0.s.en: (1) The accusation of rebellion against Nehemiah

6.0.0.en: The enemies of Nehemiah heard that he had been able to build the whole wall and that no breach remained in it, that is, it had become complete, and nothing remained but for him to make the gates of the city and set up their doors (leaves). They were greatly distressed and felt that their four previous plots had failed, which are mentioned in (chs. 2, 4), and they are:

6.0.1.en: 1- Accusing the Jews of rebelling against the empire (ch. 2:19).

6.0.2.en: 2- Mocking the Jews and despising the wall that they were building (ch. 4:1).

6.0.3.en: 3- Plotting a war to attack Jerusalem and thereby hinder the building of the wall (ch. 4:8).

6.0.4.en: 4- Weakening the resolve of the Jewish builders by sending Jews who were informants for the enemies (ch. 4:10).

6.1.0.en: The plain of Ono: a village in the tribe of Benjamin, lying on the border of the tribe of Benjamin and the land of Samaria, north of Jerusalem at a distance of 32 km.

6.1.1.en: Two of Nehemiah's enemies, Sanballat and Geshem, sent to Nehemiah asking him to come to the plain of Ono to negotiate with him, saying that there were accusations directed against him and they did not want these accusations to reach the king. In truth they intended to kill Nehemiah on the way, or to seize him in the village of Ono. The deceit of the enemies appears in the fact that the village of Ono has no walls, so that Nehemiah would be reassured that they did not want to detain him in a walled city, whereas in truth they did not want to negotiate but to seize him or kill him. And if they could not, they would at least hinder the building of the wall, even if only for a few days, the days of negotiation.

6.2.0.en: Negotiating with the wicked is of no benefit, but harmful. This is what Eve fell into when she negotiated and conversed with the serpent, and fell. Therefore we see Nehemiah refusing to negotiate, occupied with the positive work, which was building the wall.

6.2.1.en: And we find Nehemiah saying, "I am doing a great work," which shows his sense of responsibility for the work and his absorption in it so as to complete it for God's sake; that is, with all his heart he is bound to the service of God. Although Nehemiah understood the evil plan of his enemies, which was an attempt to kill him or seize him, he gave a logical reason for refusing to negotiate, namely his being occupied with building the wall, which would be hindered if he left it to negotiate with them.

6.3.0.en: When Nehemiah refused to negotiate with the enemies, they repeated their request; that is, they invited him four times to negotiate, but he kept refusing, for he was firm in holding to the positive work. Of course their insistence shows their evil, just as Satan presses us to commit sin.

6.3.1.en: The evil of the enemies is clear, because if they had been sincere in their love they would have come to him in Jerusalem. Nehemiah's holding fast to staying in Jerusalem, which is the holy place and signifies the strong fortress, was good. Nehemiah offered nothing in answer to the enemies' request but the excuse of being occupied in building the wall; he was occupied in the service of God, and did not speak of the evil of the enemies, so as not to waste his time in foolish arguments.

6.4.0.en: Sanballat sent a fifth message and invitation to Nehemiah to negotiate. At this stage the invitation was not an oral message but a written letter. Letters in ancient times were written on parchment, that is, thin skin, and sometimes on papyrus, and were delivered as follows:

6.4.1.en: 1- Either they were rolled up and sealed and put inside a box, to be kept secret and out of respect for the person to whom it was sent.

6.4.2.en: 2- Or they were not sealed and not put in a box, so that anyone could read them before they reached their owner. Sanballat sent the letter in the second way, and this means two things.

6.4.3.en: a- Contempt for Nehemiah, because the sealing of a letter means the greatness of the one to whom it is sent.

6.4.4.en: b- So that the people would read it before it reached Nehemiah, and doubt and fear and press Nehemiah to negotiate with Sanballat, and so the work would stop.

6.4.5.en: By this method Sanballat intended to disturb Nehemiah so that he would do one of these things:

6.4.6.en: 1- Fear and the abandonment of building the wall.

6.4.7.en: 2- Fear and hastening to negotiate with Sanballat, because the letter contained the accusation of Nehemiah that he wanted to set himself up as king and rebel against the king of Persia.

6.4.8.en: 3- Traveling to the king to declare his innocence, so that the work would stop.

6.4.9.en: 4- Accusing the people of taking part in the rebellion, so that they would fear and not help Nehemiah in building the wall. Sanballat accused Nehemiah of having appointed prophets in Jerusalem to proclaim him king in Jerusalem, to make it and Judea independent of the king of Persia. This accusation was based on the fact that Malachi in the third chapter of his prophecy spoke of the awaited Messiah. So Sanballat accused Nehemiah of having appointed this Malachi and others to help in setting him up as king, since the Messiah in Sanballat's view was Nehemiah.

6.4.10.en: Sanballat claimed that the Gentile nations around the Jews were saying that Nehemiah wanted to set himself up as king, and that Geshem the Arabian, one of Nehemiah's enemies and one of the great and well-known figures, had heard this talk and told Sanballat of it. And Sanballat comes forward to Nehemiah as a friend to negotiate with him, to protect him from these reports. All this was a lie and pretense on Sanballat's part, to frighten Nehemiah and hinder the building.

6.5.0.en: In faith in God Nehemiah answered Sanballat that his words were a lie and an untrue pretense. Nehemiah's answer was in these brief words because he was occupied with his aim, which was building the wall, so as to complete it as soon as possible.

6.6.0.en: The threats and fears sent to Nehemiah increased, along with false claims that the Jews were afraid and that their interest and strength in the building were weak, but he was not shaken, and did two important things:

6.6.1.en: 1- He prayed to God and asked for His help and strengthening.

6.6.2.en: 2- He made a vow to God to complete the work, and here Nehemiah's determination to complete the building is understood implicitly, and he asks God to strengthen him.

6.6.3.en: Hold fast to your spiritual striving and every building work you do, and rely on prayer. Then you will not be disturbed by Satan's hindrances that try to trouble you and take you away from God.

6.7.0.en: After the failure of the fifth attempt to stop the building of the wall, which was luring Nehemiah to negotiate with Sanballat, mentioned in (vv. 1-9), the enemies plotted the sixth and last plot to hinder the building, but God exposed it to Nehemiah and helped him until he completed the wall.

6.7.1.en: The sixth plot was extremely dangerous, for it was a carefully planned scheme. Shemaiah invited Nehemiah to visit him in his house. This Shemaiah was considered a great prophet in Israel, and it seems that he spent many periods in seclusion in his house, as shown by his saying that his house was shut up. Because of Shemaiah's standing, Nehemiah went to him to listen to his counsel and wisdom, which were known in Israel. Shemaiah said to him, showing friendship and concern for him, that Tobiah and the rest of the enemies were trying to kill him, and this was clear from the previous plots. He suggested to him a way to escape from their hand: that he go with him to the temple and hide there and they shut the doors on themselves, so that the enemies could not reach Nehemiah, because the temple had doorkeepers and guards, in addition to its being forbidden to any non-Jew to enter the temple. Then Shemaiah's suggestion was to enter into the midst of the temple, meaning by this the Holy Place, where only the priests enter, so the enemies could not reach him. It appears from Shemaiah's words that he was telling him of a specific plot that he had learned of, either by divine counsel or through his contact with the people, who considered him and honored him, so they could convey news to him.

6.7.2.en: Shemaiah's plot appears to be carefully planned, since Shemaiah was in his shut-up house to suggest to Nehemiah that he was in seclusion, so divine revelations might be expected to have reached him. And Shemaiah's specifying the time of the enemies' attempt to kill Nehemiah, namely at night, confirms to Nehemiah that it is a divine revelation.

6.7.3.en: And Shemaiah's summoning Nehemiah to his shut-up house suggests to Nehemiah that the words are secret and serious, in addition to their being a divine revelation, as we said.

6.7.4.en: Shemaiah exploited in these words Nehemiah's love for God, and therefore his taking refuge in the temple would be a thing dear to him. But this plot had a flaw, which is that it was not right for Nehemiah to enter the midst of the temple, because he was not a priest, and his entering would be against the Law of God.

6.8.0.en: God revealed to Nehemiah the plot of Shemaiah, and most likely Nehemiah had lifted up a prayer to God, who guided him how to act. He rejected Shemaiah's suggestion for the following reasons:

6.8.1.en: 1- His submitting to Shemaiah's suggestion would declare that he was afraid of the enemies, and this conflicts with faith, so God would be displeased with him and he would lose His protection and care.

6.8.2.en: 2- Nehemiah's hiding and fear would make fear creep into the hearts of his people, so they too would flee and leave off completing the wall, that is, making the gates, which would expose Jerusalem to the enemies' attack.

6.8.3.en: 3- Nehemiah's entering the midst of the temple, that is, the Holy Place, which no one is allowed to enter except the priests, would greatly provoke God against him, in addition to provoking the anger of the priests against him, because they held fast to the Law, and by this division would occur, and this would stop the completion of the wall.

6.8.4.en: 4- Nehemiah is a responsible person who wants to complete the wall whatever the cost, even if it were his life. He is ready to complete the work even if he died for the sake of God and his people, and in this he is a type of Christ the Redeemer.

6.9.0.en: When Nehemiah obeyed the voice of God, which he sensed after prayer, and in faith rejected Shemaiah's counsel, ready to face death for his people, God revealed to him the plot of Shemaiah, and he became sure that his words were at the instigation of the enemies Tobiah and Sanballat, who had hired him for this base work against God and his people, and against Nehemiah the great leader, most likely in return for material gifts. Shemaiah here is a type of Judas Iscariot the traitor, who betrayed Christ his Teacher, whom Nehemiah signifies.

6.10.0.en: The enemies' purpose in Shemaiah's plot was to make Nehemiah fall into sin, so that he would abandon God, and then the disgrace of sin would come upon him, and he would lose his standing as leader of the people and become despised, and therefore be unable to lead his people in the spiritual way and in building Jerusalem and raising it up.

6.11.0.en: From this plot we discover that Nehemiah faced a severe war from the enemies by means of a group of false prophets in Jerusalem and Judea, headed by Shemaiah and Noadiah the prophetess, two false prophets who are not mentioned in the Holy Bible except here.

6.11.1.en: These prophets tried in various ways and with false prophecies to frighten Nehemiah, and they were all hired by the enemies Tobiah and Sanballat, but he held fast to God and so was able to stand firm in faith and overcome their plots.

6.11.2.en: This plot shows the enemies' insistence on fighting Nehemiah to the last moment to stop the completion of the wall, as Satan does, who keeps fighting the children of God all their lives. It is noticed that Nehemiah's heart was not filled with evil toward the enemies, but he left the matter to God to act as He saw fit to do toward these wicked men. He is a man occupied with the positive work and has no spirit of revenge toward those who are hostile to him.

6.11.3.en: Believe in God who loves you and trust in His ability to protect you. Even in the midst of dangers lift your heart in prayer to Him in every situation, confident that He is near you and will guide you to what is for your good.

6.12.s.en: (3) The completion of the wall and Tobiah's relations

6.12.0.en: Nehemiah completed the building of the wall and its gates in fifty-two days, taking into account that they rested on the Sabbath day. It is clear that the building of the wall was done in a very short time for the following reasons:

6.12.1.en: 1- The help of God, who crowns the striving of His children with great support.

6.12.2.en: 2- The concern of all the people to take part in building the wall, so the number of workers was very great.

6.12.3.en: 3- The order and arrangement with which the building was done, for each group was responsible for repairing a specific part of the wall, that is, responsibility was assigned to each group.

6.12.4.en: 4- The wall was not all broken down but only parts of it, in addition to the fallen stones lying on the ground beside the wall, which the workers took and completed the building with.

6.12.5.en: 5- Nehemiah's and his helpers' encouragement of the people, and his leading the work himself.

6.12.6.en: The building was completed on the twenty-fifth of the month of Elul in the year 444 B.C., and this month corresponds to the month of September in the Gregorian year. Daniel had prophesied in the year 605 B.C. the completion of the building of the wall (Dan 9:25).

6.13.0.en: When Nehemiah's enemies learned that he had completed the building of the wall, they felt the following:

6.13.1.en: 1- They were ashamed and abashed and felt their weakness, since all their attempts to stop the building had failed.

6.13.2.en: 2- They envied the Jews, who were able to fortify their city Jerusalem, while the enemies' cities were not fortified like it, and they had not been able to obtain permission for this from the emperor.

6.13.3.en: 3- They were sure that this great success was by the power of God, and therefore could not be resisted; that is why all their attempts failed. But sadly they did not believe in God or fear Him, and their wars against the people of God were repeated afterward.

6.14.0.en: After the failure of Tobiah, the greatest enemy of the Jews, and the completion of the building of the wall, Tobiah did not surrender but kept fighting the people of God with cunning and malice by means of:

6.14.1.en: 1- Relations with the chiefs of the tribe of Judah, and even an alliance with them, and perhaps this was through gifts that Tobiah gave to the chiefs, as shown by their testimony to him in (v. 19).

6.14.2.en: 2- The intermarriage of the Jews with foreign women of the Gentiles, from the sons and daughters of Tobiah and Sanballat, so the sons of Tobiah married the children of the chiefs of Judah, Shechaniah and Meshullam. By this intermarriage Tobiah was able to learn the news of the Jews, and even to spread among them whatever news he wanted in order to influence them and weaken them.

6.14.3.en: 3- The passing of many letters from the chiefs of Judah to Tobiah and the reverse, which made Tobiah know the news of the Jews and influence them also.

6.14.4.en: 4- By Tobiah's relations he influenced many of the chiefs of Judah, so they began to praise Tobiah before Nehemiah as a generous and great man who loved the Jews, although he was deceitful and established these relations for his own benefit and gave gifts to deceive and win the chiefs of Judah.

6.14.5.en: 5- When the attempts to praise Tobiah before Nehemiah failed, Tobiah began to send reports to frighten Nehemiah, to make him lose his ability to lead and be shaken before his people.

6.14.6.en: Do not be disturbed by the continuing wars of Satan, for they are worthless before the power of God that is in you, and do not be disturbed either by the deception of many of the loved ones around you by the ideas of the world, but be steadfast in God's commandments and all you learned in the Church, confident that God who is in you is stronger than all the power of the demons, your enemies. The guarding of Jerusalem and the genealogies of the people. After Nehemiah's success in building the wall he was encouraged to enter into other positive works, so he took care to guard the city, and then took care also of the people living in Jerusalem, so he searched out their genealogies, especially of the priests and Levites, to care for the service of the temple and to establish the people spiritually with God. So after Nehemiah's success in the external work, which was the wall, he took care of the internal work, which was the guarding of the city and the spiritual life of its inhabitants. For whoever begins to work gains the positive spirit in all his life. Chapters 1-6 speak about the building of the wall, and from chapter 7 to the end of the book they tell us about the building of the people.
